title: attentionpredictor.com first screen: UI/UX/CRO attention benchmark
goal: For attentionpredictor.com the intended approach is message-led (the promise comes first, the product demo second), so it is validated against the 27 top-SaaS pages built that way on desktop and 58 on mobile. The approach was not stated by the owner; it is the one the page follows today.
verdict: Nothing key is in a blind spot. As a message-led page the first screen does its main job: the headline (32.2%) and the message block (38.0%) sit above the range of the reference pages (13.9–25.2% and 18.4–29.5%), and the primary CTA (1.0%) is inside its range (0.9–1.8%). Three things fall short of the group: the action block as a whole is below range (1.5% vs 2.1–4.4%), the secondary "API" button is a blind spot (0.5% vs 1.0–1.6%), and there is no header CTA (23 of 27 reference pages have one). The message has budget to spare: giving 3–5 points to the action block would still leave it at the top of its range. On mobile every key and supporting element is in or above range.
top_actions: Fix the blind spot: replace the one-word "API" button with a named secondary action ("Read the docs") at the same height as the primary. Target: 1.0–1.6% desktop (today 0.5%).

Bring the action block into range: a ~1.5× larger primary button with a specific label and one line of microcopy. Target: 2.1–4.4% desktop (today 1.5%), paid for by the headline (32% → about 28%, still above its range).
Add a header CTA: 23 of 27 message-led reference pages have one. Target: 0.2–0.3% desktop.
Leave the headline, subhead and the mobile first screen alone: they are in or above range; pushing them higher would take attention from the action block.
Decide on the demo image: it is optional for a message-led page. Moving it up is a change of approach (to balanced), not a fix - see the approach notes.
approach_notes: Why message-led: message 38.0% vs hero visual 15.0% on desktop (2.5 : 1); on mobile there is no hero visual in the first screen at all.

What the spread says: 30.0% of desktop attention sits in a different block than in the reference group. Most of that is healthy for this approach (more on the message, less on empty background: 38% unassigned vs 61%); the part to correct is action (1.5% vs 3.6% mean) and header (3.2% vs 8.1%).

If the owner wanted a balanced page instead (message and product demo sharing the screen; 36 reference pages), the picture changes: the hero visual would be a blind spot (15.0% vs 19.4–31.0%). That is a redesign of the first screen, so choose the approach first and optimise second.
Distance from poorly made pages: their median headline share is 8.5% and message block 10.7% on desktop; this page is far above both.
target_notes: Message dominates by design: headline 32.2% + subhead 5.5% + eyebrow 0.4% = 38%; attention per area of the headline (2.2) shows it is both big and attractive.
Headline gives attention back over time: 32.2% at 3 s → 27.3% at 10 s; attention then moves to the demo images (15.0 → 18.7%), not to the CTAs (1.5 → 1.7%).
CTAs are small, not unattractive: "Talk to us" covers 0.4% of the screen and "API" 0.2%; both have high attention per area (2.4, 2.0), so size and wording are the levers, not colour.
Proof stats: the 1.7M sessions / 34M fixations / MAE chips get 4.2%, inside the range of the 8 reference pages that show proof (3.3–4.9%). They are optional and sized right.
benchmark_notes: For context only: among the 100 top-SaaS pages attentionpredictor.com would rank 3rd on headline share and 4th on message share on desktop. That is a consequence of the message-led approach, not a target in itself.

Message-led pages that pair a strong message (over 25%) with an in-range action block: Stripe (30.4% / 2.4%), GitLab (32.8% / 2.3%), 1Password (38.5% / 2.2%), ZoomInfo (30.9% / 3.6%), PandaDoc (28.6% / 2.3%), Asana (25.9% / 3.6%).
The hero visual gets 15.0%, more than any of the 7 message-led reference pages that show one (4.1–8.4%); for a message-led page that is acceptable as long as the action block is fixed first.
mobile_notes: Validated as message-led against 58 reference pages. Message (44.6%), headline (26.2%) and subhead (17.4%) are above range; action block (9.3% vs 4.9–13.8%), primary CTA (5.2% vs 3.4–6.4%) and secondary CTA (4.1% vs 2.7–6.2%) are in range.
The three stats cards take 11.5%, above the range of the 7 reference pages that show proof (4.6–8.6%). They are optional; if the action block ever needs more, take it from here.
No header CTA on mobile; only 25 of 58 reference pages have one, so it is not counted as missing.
Nothing on mobile needs fixing first; carry over the secondary-CTA wording from desktop for consistency.

guidelines.title: G1 · Fix the blind spot: the secondary CTA
points: Replace "API" with a named action: "Read the docs" or "See the API reference".
Same height as the primary, outline style, directly beside it.
Takes attention from: the headline (see G2).
guidelines.target: secondary CTA 1.0–1.6% desktop (today 0.5%); stay inside 2.7–6.2% on mobile (today 4.1%).
guidelines.evidence: desktop: under the 10th percentile (0.7%) of the 12 reference pages with a secondary CTA; box area 0.2% of the screen with good attention per area (2.0), so it is too small, not unattractive.

guidelines.title: G2 · Bring the action block into range
points: Primary: specific value label ("Get API access", "Try it on your image") instead of "Talk to us"; ≈ 180×52 px.
One line of true, risk-reducing microcopy under the buttons.
Takes attention from: the headline. Tighten it to 2 lines (≈ 64–70 px); 32% → about 28% keeps it above its range (13.9–25.2%).
guidelines.target: action block 2.1–4.4% desktop (today 1.5%); keep mobile inside 4.9–13.8% (today 9.3%).
guidelines.evidence: action block below the p25 of 27 message-led reference pages; primary CTA alone is in range (1.0% vs 0.9–1.8%), so the gap is the secondary button and missing microcopy.

guidelines.title: G3 · Add a header CTA
points: A filled "Get API access" button at the right end of the nav.
Optional on mobile (25 of 58 reference pages have one).
guidelines.evidence: 23 of 27 message-led reference pages show a nav CTA; the target has none.

guidelines.title: G4 · Keep what is in range
points: Headline wording and prominence, subhead, proof chips, the whole mobile first screen.
Do not enlarge the headline further: it is already above range and every extra point comes from action or proof.
guidelines.target: headline stays ≥ 25% desktop, ≥ 23% mobile (top of the reference range).

guidelines.title: G5 · Validate
points: Mock the variant (G1–G3), score it with this skill and check that every key element is in range and nothing new fell into a blind spot.
Then run a live A/B test on API sign-ups / contact requests.
guidelines.evidence: predicted attention screens designs; it does not prove conversion.

limits: The target was scored in a different Attention Predictor workspace than part of the benchmark (same model).
Ranges for optional elements rest on few reference pages (7–12) and are indicative.
